pharm: Antagonizes dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors (with activity at other serotonergic, adrenergic, and histaminergic receptors); the exact mechanism in bipolar disorder is unknown
quick: Bipolar adjunct: 5 mg sublingually twice daily, up to 10 mg twice daily
Sublingual - do not eat or drink for 10 minutes after dosing
Third-trimester exposure risks neonatal EPS/withdrawal; pregnancy registry available
Unknown if in human milk; weigh benefit and risk
No dosage adjustment needed for renal impairment
Contraindicated in severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment
Weight, glucose, lipids, BP/orthostasis, EPS, CBC, ECG/QT
summary: Asenapine is a sublingual atypical antipsychotic. In this labeling it is indicated for bipolar I disorder - acute monotherapy of manic or mixed episodes in pediatric patients 10 to 17 years and as adjunct to lithium or valproate in adults. The tablet dissolves under the tongue in seconds and patients must avoid eating or drinking for 10 minutes. It carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis and is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.
indications: Bipolar I disorder - acute monotherapy of manic or mixed episodes in pediatric patients 10 to 17 years of age
Bipolar I disorder - adjunctive treatment to lithium or valproate in adults

dosage.d: Start 5 mg sublingually twice daily; usual 5 to 10 mg twice daily
Start 2.5 mg twice daily; after 3 days increase to 5 mg twice daily; after 3 more days may increase to 10 mg twice daily
dosage.n: Follow escalation schedule (sensitivity to dystonia); max 10 mg twice daily; doses above this not evaluated
Asenapine exposure is markedly increased in severe hepatic impairment

admin: Place the tablet under the tongue and allow it to dissolve completely (dissolves in saliva within seconds)
Do not split, crush, chew, or swallow the tablet
Do not eat or drink for 10 minutes after administration (water shortly after reduces exposure)
Follow the recommended dose-escalation schedule, particularly in pediatric patients (dystonia risk)
moa: Asenapine is an atypical antipsychotic; the mechanism of action in bipolar I disorder is unknown. Its efficacy is thought to be mediated through combined antagonist activity at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional activity at other serotonergic, adrenergic (alpha-1), and histaminergic (H1) receptors.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to asenapine or any formulation component (reactions have included anaphylaxis, angioedema, hypotension, tachycardia, swollen tongue, dyspnea, wheezing, rash)
relative: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (increased mortality and cerebrovascular events - not approved for this use)
Cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease, risk of dehydration or syncope (orthostatic hypotension)
Pre-existing low WBC or history of leukopenia/neutropenia
Risk factors for QT prolongation; history of seizures
monitor: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipids (metabolic effects)
Blood pressure and orthostatic vital signs
CBC in patients with pre-existing low WBC; ECG/QT in at-risk patients

preg: Studies have not been conducted in pregnant women and there are no available human data on the drug-associated risk. Neonates exposed to antipsychotics during the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder), which may require prolonged hospitalization. A pregnancy exposure registry (National Pregnancy Registry for Atypical Antipsychotics, 1-866-961-2388) monitors outcomes. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk to a fetus.
lact: There are limited data on the presence of asenapine in human milk; asenapine is present in the milk of lactating animals. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment based on the labeling.
hepatic: Asenapine is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), where exposure is markedly increased. No dose adjustment is needed for mild to moderate hepatic impairment per labeling.

major: QT-prolonging drugs - avoid concomitant use (additive QT prolongation)
moderate: Antihypertensive drugs - asenapine has alpha-1 antagonism and may enhance hypotension; monitor BP and adjust
Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g. fluvoxamine) - increase asenapine exposure; asenapine dose reduction may be needed
Paroxetine (CYP2D6 substrate/inhibitor) - asenapine doubles paroxetine exposure; reduce paroxetine dose by half
CNS depressants and alcohol - additive sedation
minor: No dosage adjustment needed with imipramine, cimetidine, valproate, lithium, or CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin)
interactions.food: Sublingual administration; avoid eating or drinking for 10 minutes after dosing (reduces absorption)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive central nervous system depression
interactions.diagnostics: May raise prolactin; monitor metabolic parameters and ECG/QT

serious: Metabolic changes - hyperglycemia/diabetes, dyslipidemia, weight gain
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including swollen tongue and airway compromise
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status)
Anaphylaxis / angioedema with swollen tongue and dyspnea
Stroke / TIA in elderly with dementia-related psychosis

monitoring: Body weight, fasting glucose/HbA1c, and lipid panel
Blood pressure and orthostatic vital signs
Complete blood count (especially with low WBC history)
Extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, and signs of NMS
counsel: Place the tablet under your tongue and let it dissolve fully - do not chew, crush, or swallow it
Do not eat or drink for 10 minutes after the dose, or it may not work properly
You may feel numbness or tingling of the mouth/tongue; this usually passes
Rise slowly to avoid dizziness/fainting, and avoid alcohol
Report fever with muscle stiffness, swelling of the tongue or trouble breathing, or uncontrolled movements
pk: Rapidly absorbed sublingually; peak within 0.5 to 1.5 hours
Tmax about 1 hour; absolute sublingual bioavailability ~35% (under 2% if swallowed)
Twice-daily dosing; steady state within about 3 days
Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C (59-86 F)
pearls: Boxed warning: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis - not approved for that use
Sublingual only; swallowing the tablet gives under 2% bioavailability, and eating/drinking within 10 minutes reduces absorption
Oral hypoesthesia (mouth/tongue numbness) is a characteristic, usually transient, effect; rare swollen tongue/airway hypersensitivity can be serious
Contraindicated in severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment; no adjustment for renal impairment
Halve the paroxetine dose when combined; the broader asenapine (Saphris) label also covers acute and maintenance treatment of schizophrenia in adults
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the regular twice-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once. Confirm the plan with your clinician.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Obtain an ECG and provide supportive care - maintain airway, oxygenation, and ventilation, and manage symptoms (reported overdose effects include agitation and confusion). Treat hypotension/circulatory collapse with IV fluids and/or sympathomimetics, but avoid epinephrine and dopamine (beta stimulation may worsen hypotension in the setting of asenapine alpha-blockade). Give anticholinergics for severe extrapyramidal symptoms. Consider multiple-drug involvement and consult a poison control center.
